en.content: If Pauli exclusion principle is not applicable and one orbital has three electrons, then last electrons of N2 molecule will be present in......
en.explanation:
Answer: (D) $\pi 2p_y$ orbital

A nitrogen molecule has a total of $14$ electrons ($7$ from each N atom). These electrons are filled into the molecular orbitals in order of increasing energy:

$$\sigma 1s < \sigma^* 1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^* 2s < \pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y < \sigma 2p_z$$

Normally each orbital takes only $2$ electrons because of the Pauli exclusion principle. But here we are told that this restriction is removed and every orbital can hold $3$ electrons. So the capacity of each molecular orbital becomes three instead of two.

Now fill the electrons:

$\sigma 1s \to 3$ electrons

$\sigma^* 1s \to 3$ electrons

$\sigma 2s \to 3$ electrons

$\sigma^* 2s \to 3$ electrons

That accounts for $3+3+3+3 = 12$ electrons.

Only $2$ electrons are left, and the next available orbitals are the two degenerate $\pi$ orbitals, $\pi 2p_x$ and $\pi 2p_y$. Since these have equal energy, Hund's rule still applies, so the electrons go in singly — one into $\pi 2p_x$ and the last one into $\pi 2p_y$.

So the configuration becomes

$$\sigma 1s^3\ \sigma^* 1s^3\ \sigma 2s^3\ \sigma^* 2s^3\ \pi 2p_x^1\ \pi 2p_y^1$$

The last electron therefore sits in the $\pi 2p_y$ orbital.

A small point worth noticing: the $\pi^* 2p_y$ orbital is antibonding and lies much higher in energy, so electrons can reach it only after the bonding $\pi$ and $\sigma 2p_z$ orbitals are filled. With only $14$ electrons and larger orbital capacity, the filling stops well before that.

options.content: If there is a nodal plane perpendicular to the internuclear axis and lying between the nuclei of bonded atoms, then the corresponding orbital is an antibonding M.O.
If a nodal plane lies in the internuclear axis, then the corresponding orbitals are pi(π) bonding M.O.
The σ-bonding molecular orbital does not contain nodal planes containing the internuclear axis.
The δ-bonding molecular orbital possesses three nodal planes containing the internuclear axis.

en.explanation:
A. This option is correct because the defining characteristic of an antibonding molecular orbital $\left(\sigma^*\right.$ or $\left.\pi^*\right)$ is the presence of a nodal plane between the two nuclei, perpendicular to the internuclear axis. This plane represents a region of zero electron density, which leads to nuclear repulsion rather than bonding.

B. This option is correct because a $\pi$-bonding MO has one nodal plane which contains the internuclear axis. Here, the electron density lies above and below the axis.

C. This option is correct because a $\sigma$-bonding MO is cylindrically symmetric about the internuclear axis and has no nodal plane containing the axis.

D. This is an incorrect option because a $\delta$-bonding MO has two nodal planes containing the internuclear axis, not three.

Answer: D

en.content: Which of the following will form hydrogen bond with another molecule of same substance?
en.explanation:
The correct option is C: $H_3PO_4$.

Hydrogen bonding takes place when hydrogen is directly attached to a highly electronegative atom like $F$, $O$, or $N$. The molecule should also have a lone pair on an electronegative atom so that another molecule can attract that hydrogen.

In $H_3PO_4$ phosphoric acid, the structure has $O-H$ bonds:

$$ H_3PO_4 \text{ has } P-OH \text{ groups} $$

Here, hydrogen is directly bonded to oxygen. Oxygen is highly electronegative and also has lone pairs. So one molecule of $H_3PO_4$ can form hydrogen bonds with another molecule of $H_3PO_4$.

Checking the other options:

$CH_2Cl_2$ has hydrogen attached to carbon, not to $F$, $O$, or $N$, so it does not form hydrogen bonding with itself.

$H_3COCH_3$, or $CH_3OCH_3$, has an oxygen atom, but no hydrogen is directly attached to oxygen. So it cannot form hydrogen bonds with another molecule of the same substance.

$PH_3$ has $P-H$ bonds, but phosphorus is not electronegative enough to form strong hydrogen bonding like $N$, $O$, or $F$.

So, the substance that forms hydrogen bonds with another molecule of the same substance is:

$$ \boxed{H_3PO_4} $$

en.content: Which orbitals of two atoms produce δ-bond (four lobe interaction)?
en.explanation:
The correct choice is Option D, but it should be read as

$$ d_{xz} \;\rightarrow\; \text{overlap along } y\text{-axis} \;\leftarrow\; d_{xz} $$

A $\delta$-bond is formed by sidewise overlap of two $d$-orbitals in such a way that four lobes interact.

For a $\delta$-bond, the internuclear axis should not pass through the lobes directly. Instead, the lobes should lie around the axis, giving four regions of overlap.

Here, if the bond axis is the $y$-axis, then the orbital $d_{xz}$ is suitable because $d_{xz}$ has lobes in the $xz$-plane. The $y$-axis passes between these lobes, so four-lobe sidewise overlap is possible.

So,

$$ d_{xz} - d_{xz} $$

overlap along the $y$-axis gives a $\delta$-bond.

Option A gives a $\sigma$-bond because $d_{z^2}$ overlaps directly along the $z$-axis.

Option B gives $\pi$-type overlap along the $x$-axis.

Option C has lobes along the $y$-axis, so it is not the usual $\delta$ overlap.

Also, $d_{xx}$ is not a standard $d$-orbital. So Option D is correct only if the second orbital is meant to be $d_{xz}$.

en.content: The polarizability of the anions changes as
en.explanation:
Polarizability means how easily the electron cloud of an anion can be distorted.

An anion becomes more polarizable when:

  • its size is larger,

  • its negative charge is higher,

  • its effective nuclear attraction on outer electrons is weaker.

Now check the options.

For option A:

$$ \text{Cl}^- ,\ \text{S}^{2-},\ \text{P}^{3-} $$

These three ions are isoelectronic. Each has $18$ electrons.

But their nuclear charges are different:

$$ \text{Cl} = 17,\quad \text{S} = 16,\quad \text{P} = 15 $$

In an isoelectronic series, the ion with smaller nuclear charge has larger size because the same number of electrons are held less strongly.

So the size order is:

$$ \text{Cl}^- < \text{S}^{2-} < \text{P}^{3-} $$

Hence polarizability also increases in the same order:

$$ \text{Cl}^- < \text{S}^{2-} < \text{P}^{3-} $$

So the correct option is:

$$ \boxed{\text{Option A}} $$

en.content: Which of the following does not undergo hydrolysis?
en.explanation:
1. Carbon tetrachloride ($\text{CCl}_4$):

Hydrolysis requires the central atom to accept a lone pair of electrons from a water molecule. The central carbon atom in $\text{CCl}_4$ belongs to the second period and has the electronic configuration $1s^2\, 2s^2\, 2p^2$. Because it lacks vacant $d$-orbitals in its valence shell, it cannot expand its octet to accommodate the incoming lone pair from water. Therefore, $\text{CCl}_4$ does not undergo hydrolysis.

  1. Silicon tetrachloride ($\text{SiCl}_4$):

Silicon belongs to the third period and has vacant $3d$-orbitals. It easily accepts lone pairs of electrons from water molecules and undergoes rapid hydrolysis to form silicic acid:

$$\text{SiCl}_4 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Si(OH)}_4 + 4\text{HCl}$$

  1. Sulfur hexafluoride ($\text{SF}_6$):

Although sulfur has vacant $d$-orbitals, it is surrounded by six small and highly electronegative fluorine atoms. These six fluorine atoms tightly shield the central sulfur atom, causing high steric hindrance. As a result, water molecules cannot approach the sulfur atom, making $\text{SF}_6$ chemically inert and resistant to hydrolysis.

  1. Tellurium hexafluoride ($\text{TeF}_6$):

Tellurium is a much larger atom than sulfur. Due to its larger size, the steric crowding around tellurium is significantly reduced, allowing water molecules to attack the central atom. Hence, $\text{TeF}_6$ undergoes hydrolysis easily.

Both $\text{CCl}_4$ and $\text{SF}_6$ do not undergo hydrolysis.

Correct Option: Option C

en.content: Write sum of the bond order of following species: $\mathrm{C}_2^{2-}, \mathrm{B}_2, \mathrm{NO}, \mathrm{O}_2^{+}, \mathrm{O}_2^{-}, \mathrm{Cl}_2, \mathrm{~S}_2$ [upto nearest integer]
en.explanation:
The formula for calculating bond order is:

$$\text{Bond Order} = \frac{N_b - N_a}{2}$$

where $N_b$ is the number of electrons in bonding molecular orbitals and $N_a$ is the number of electrons in antibonding molecular orbitals.

For diatomic species with up to 14 electrons, the order of filling molecular orbitals is:

$$\sigma 1s < \sigma^* 1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^* 2s < (\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y) < \sigma 2p_z < (\pi^* 2p_x = \pi^* 2p_y) < \sigma^* 2p_z$$

For species with more than 14 electrons, $\sigma 2p_z$ is filled before the $\pi 2p$ orbitals:

$$\sigma 1s < \sigma^* 1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^* 2s < \sigma 2p_z < (\pi 2p_x = \pi 2p_y) < (\pi^* 2p_x = \pi^* 2p_y) < \sigma^* 2p_z$$

  1. $\mathrm{C}_2^{2-}$

Total electrons $= 6 + 6 + 2 = 14$

Configuration: $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^* 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^* 2s^2 \pi 2p_x^2 \pi 2p_y^2 \sigma 2p_z^2$

$$\text{Bond Order} = \frac{10 - 4}{2} = 3$$

  1. $\mathrm{B}_2$

Total electrons $= 5 + 5 = 10$

Configuration: $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^* 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^* 2s^2 \pi 2p_x^1 \pi 2p_y^1$

$$\text{Bond Order} = \frac{6 - 4}{2} = 1$$

  1. $\mathrm{NO}$

Total electrons $= 7 + 8 = 15$

Configuration: $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^* 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^* 2s^2 \sigma 2p_z^2 \pi 2p_x^2 \pi 2p_y^2 \pi^* 2p_x^1$

$$\text{Bond Order} = \frac{10 - 5}{2} = 2.5$$

  1. $\mathrm{O}_2^{+}$

Total electrons $= 8 + 8 - 1 = 15$

Configuration: $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^* 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^* 2s^2 \sigma 2p_z^2 \pi 2p_x^2 \pi 2p_y^2 \pi^* 2p_x^1$

$$\text{Bond Order} = \frac{10 - 5}{2} = 2.5$$

  1. $\mathrm{O}_2^{-}$

Total electrons $= 8 + 8 + 1 = 17$

Configuration: $\sigma 1s^2 \sigma^* 1s^2 \sigma 2s^2 \sigma^* 2s^2 \sigma 2p_z^2 \pi 2p_x^2 \pi 2p_y^2 \pi^* 2p_x^2 \pi^* 2p_y^1$

$$\text{Bond Order} = \frac{10 - 7}{2} = 1.5$$

  1. $\mathrm{Cl}_2$

Chlorine forms a single covalent bond between the two atoms to complete their octets.

$$\text{Bond Order} = 1$$

  1. $\mathrm{S}_2$

$\mathrm{S}_2$ has 12 valence electrons and is isoelectronic with $\mathrm{O}_2$ in its valence shell, having two unpaired electrons in the antibonding orbitals.

$$\text{Bond Order} = 2$$

Now, adding the bond orders of all the given species:

$$\text{Sum} = 3 + 1 + 2.5 + 2.5 + 1.5 + 1 + 2 = 13.5$$

Rounding off to the nearest integer gives $14$.

en.content:
Consider the following orbitals.

(i) $3 p_x$

(ii) $4 d_{z^2}$

(iii) $3 d_{x^2-y^2}$

(iv) $3 d_{x y}$

Then, calculate the value of " $a+b+c$ ".

$a=$ Total number of grade orbitals in the above given orbitals.

$b=$ Total number of ungerade orbitals in the above given orbitals.

$c=$ Total number of axial orbitals in the above given orbitals.
en.explanation:
For atomic orbitals, gerade or ungerade character depends on the value of azimuthal quantum number $l$.

If $l$ is even, the orbital is gerade $(g)$.

If $l$ is odd, the orbital is ungerade $(u)$.

Now,

$3p_x$ is a $p$-orbital, so $l=1$.

Since $l$ is odd, $3p_x$ is ungerade.

$4d_{z^2}$, $3d_{x^2-y^2}$ and $3d_{xy}$ are all $d$-orbitals, so $l=2$.

Since $l$ is even, all these $d$-orbitals are gerade.

So,

$$ a=3 $$

and

$$ b=1 $$

Now, axial orbitals are those orbitals whose lobes lie along the coordinate axes.

Among the given orbitals:

$3p_x$ lies along the $x$-axis, so it is axial.

$4d_{z^2}$ lies along the $z$-axis, so it is axial.

$3d_{x^2-y^2}$ lies along the $x$ and $y$ axes, so it is axial.

$3d_{xy}$ lies between the axes, so it is not axial.

Thus,

$$ c=3 $$

Hence,

$$ a+b+c=3+1+3=7 $$

So, the value of $a+b+c$ is

$$ \boxed{7} $$

en.content: Among $\mathrm{H}_2, \mathrm{He}_2^{+}, \mathrm{Li}_2, \mathrm{Be}_2, \mathrm{C}_2, \mathrm{~N}_2, \mathrm{O}_2^{-}$and $\mathrm{F}_2$, the number of diamagnetic species is: (Atomic number): $(\mathrm{H}=1, \mathrm{He}=2, \mathrm{Li}=3, \mathrm{Be}=4, \mathrm{C}=6, \mathrm{~N}=7, \mathrm{O}=8, \mathrm{~F}=9)$
en.explanation:
A species is diamagnetic when all electrons are paired in its molecular orbital configuration.

For $\mathrm{H}_2$:

$$ \mathrm{H}_2: \sigma_{1s}^2 $$

Both electrons are paired, so $\mathrm{H}_2$ is diamagnetic.

For $\mathrm{He}_2^+$, total electrons $= 3$:

$$ \mathrm{He}_2^+: \sigma_{1s}^2 \, \sigma_{1s}^{*1} $$

One electron is unpaired, so $\mathrm{He}_2^+$ is paramagnetic.

For $\mathrm{Li}_2$:

$$ \mathrm{Li}_2: \sigma_{1s}^2 \, \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \, \sigma_{2s}^2 $$

All electrons are paired, so $\mathrm{Li}_2$ is diamagnetic.

For $\mathrm{Be}_2$:

$$ \mathrm{Be}_2: \sigma_{1s}^2 \, \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \, \sigma_{2s}^2 \, \sigma_{2s}^{*2} $$

All electrons are paired, so $\mathrm{Be}_2$ is diamagnetic.

Its bond order is zero, so it is not stable, but based on electron pairing it is diamagnetic.

For $\mathrm{C}_2$, the order of filling for molecules up to $\mathrm{N}_2$ is:

$$ \sigma_{2s},\ \sigma_{2s}^*,\ \pi_{2p_x}=\pi_{2p_y},\ \sigma_{2p_z} $$

So,

$$ \mathrm{C}_2: \sigma_{2s}^2 \, \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \, \pi_{2p_x}^2 \, \pi_{2p_y}^2 $$

All electrons are paired, so $\mathrm{C}_2$ is diamagnetic.

For $\mathrm{N}_2$:

$$ \mathrm{N}_2: \sigma_{2s}^2 \, \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \, \pi_{2p_x}^2 \, \pi_{2p_y}^2 \, \sigma_{2p_z}^2 $$

All electrons are paired, so $\mathrm{N}_2$ is diamagnetic.

For $\mathrm{O}_2^-$, oxygen and fluorine follow the order:

$$ \sigma_{2s},\ \sigma_{2s}^*,\ \sigma_{2p_z},\ \pi_{2p_x}=\pi_{2p_y},\ \pi_{2p_x}^*=\pi_{2p_y}^* $$

$\mathrm{O}_2^-$ has one extra electron compared to $\mathrm{O}_2$. In the antibonding $\pi^*$ orbitals, one electron remains unpaired:

$$ \pi_{2p_x}^{*2} \, \pi_{2p_y}^{*1} $$

So $\mathrm{O}_2^-$ is paramagnetic.

For $\mathrm{F}_2$:

$$ \mathrm{F}_2: \sigma_{2s}^2 \, \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \, \sigma_{2p_z}^2 \, \pi_{2p_x}^2 \, \pi_{2p_y}^2 \, \pi_{2p_x}^{*2} \, \pi_{2p_y}^{*2} $$

All electrons are paired, so $\mathrm{F}_2$ is diamagnetic.

Diamagnetic species are:

$$ \mathrm{H}_2,\ \mathrm{Li}_2,\ \mathrm{Be}_2,\ \mathrm{C}_2,\ \mathrm{N}_2,\ \mathrm{F}_2 $$

Hence, the number of diamagnetic species is

$$ \boxed{6} $$

en.content:
Set A : Among the species, $\mathrm{NO}, \mathrm{CO}$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$ the number of species will undergo an increase in bond order on ionisation is ' $x$ '.

Set B : Among the species, $\mathrm{O}_2, \mathrm{O}_2^{+}, \mathrm{O}_2^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{O}_2^{2-}$, the number of species which will not show a change in its magnetic behaviour on ionisation is ' $y$ '.

The value of $x+y$ is $\_\_\_\_$
en.explanation:
Ionisation involves the removal of one electron from the neutral or ionic species ($\text{M} \rightarrow \text{M}^+ + \text{e}^-$).

The bond order is given by:

$$\text{Bond Order} = \frac{N_b - N_a}{2}$$

where $N_b$ is the number of bonding electrons and $N_a$ is the number of antibonding electrons.

Finding the value of $x$ (Set A)

We check the effect of removing one electron on the bond order for each species:

  • $\mathrm{NO}$ (15 electrons):

  • Configuration: $\sigma_{1s}^2 \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \sigma_{2s}^2 \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \sigma_{2p_z}^2 \pi_{2p_x}^2 \pi_{2p_y}^2 \pi_{2p_x}^{*1}$

  • $\text{Bond Order of } \mathrm{NO} = \frac{10 - 5}{2} = 2.5$

  • On ionisation to $\mathrm{NO}^+$ (14 electrons), the electron is removed from the antibonding orbital ($\pi_{2p}^*$).

  • $\text{Bond Order of } \mathrm{NO}^+ = \frac{10 - 4}{2} = 3.0$ (Increases)

  • $\mathrm{CO}$ (14 electrons):

  • Configuration: $\sigma_{1s}^2 \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \sigma_{2s}^2 \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \pi_{2p_x}^2 \pi_{2p_y}^2 \sigma_{2p_z}^2$

  • $\text{Bond Order of } \mathrm{CO} = \frac{10 - 4}{2} = 3.0$

  • On ionisation to $\mathrm{CO}^+$ (13 electrons), an electron is removed from a bonding orbital ($\sigma_{2p_z}$).

  • $\text{Bond Order of } \mathrm{CO}^+ = \frac{9 - 4}{2} = 2.5$ (Decreases)

  • $\mathrm{O}_2$ (16 electrons):

  • Configuration: $\sigma_{1s}^2 \sigma_{1s}^{*2} \sigma_{2s}^2 \sigma_{2s}^{*2} \sigma_{2p_z}^2 \pi_{2p_x}^2 \pi_{2p_y}^2 \pi_{2p_x}^{*1} \pi_{2p_y}^{*1}$

  • $\text{Bond Order of } \mathrm{O}_2 = \frac{10 - 6}{2} = 2.0$

  • On ionisation to $\mathrm{O}_2^+$ (15 electrons), the electron is removed from the antibonding orbital ($\pi_{2p}^*$).

  • $\text{Bond Order of } \mathrm{O}_2^+ = \frac{10 - 5}{2} = 2.5$ (Increases)

The species showing an increase in bond order on ionisation are $\mathrm{NO}$ and $\mathrm{O}_2$.

$$x = 2$$

Finding the value of $y$ (Set B)

We check the magnetic nature before and after ionisation:

  • $\mathrm{O}_2$ (16 electrons) $\rightarrow \mathrm{O}_2^+$ (15 electrons):

  • $\mathrm{O}_2$ has 2 unpaired electrons (Paramagnetic).

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^+$ has 1 unpaired electron (Paramagnetic).

  • Magnetic behaviour remains the same (No change).

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^+$ (15 electrons) $\rightarrow \mathrm{O}_2^{2+}$ (14 electrons):

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^+$ is Paramagnetic.

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^{2+}$ has 0 unpaired electrons (Diamagnetic).

  • Magnetic behaviour changes.

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^{2+}$ (14 electrons) $\rightarrow \mathrm{O}_2^{3+}$ (13 electrons):

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^{2+}$ is Diamagnetic.

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^{3+}$ has 1 unpaired electron (Paramagnetic).

  • Magnetic behaviour changes.

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^{2-}$ (18 electrons) $\rightarrow \mathrm{O}_2^-$ (17 electrons):

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^{2-}$ is Diamagnetic.

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^-$ has 1 unpaired electron (Paramagnetic).

  • Magnetic behaviour changes.

Only $\mathrm{O}_2$ does not show a change in its magnetic behaviour.

$$y = 1$$

Value of $x + y$

$$x + y = 2 + 1 = 3$$

en.content:
Total number of species which has/have symmetrical electronic distribution in their HOMO and also paramagnetic.

$$ \mathrm{N}_2^{+}, \mathrm{O}_2^{2-}, \mathrm{C}_2, \mathrm{O}_2, \mathrm{~B}_2, \mathrm{C}_2^{2-}, \mathrm{N}_2^{2-} $$
en.explanation:
1. For species with $\le 14$ electrons: $\sigma_{1s} < \sigma^*_{1s} < \sigma_{2s} < \sigma^*_{2s} < (\pi_{2p_x} = \pi_{2p_y}) < \sigma_{2p_z}$

  2. For species with $> 14$ electrons: $\sigma_{1s} < \sigma^*_{1s} < \sigma_{2s} < \sigma^*_{2s} < \sigma_{2p_z} < (\pi_{2p_x} = \pi_{2p_y}) < (\pi^*_{2p_x} = \pi^*_{2p_y})$

Here is the step-by-step breakdown for the solution field:

MO Configuration and Analysis

  • $\mathrm{N}_2^+$ ($13e^-$):

$$\dots \sigma_{2s}^2 \sigma_{2s}^{*2} (\pi_{2p_x}^2 = \pi_{2p_y}^2) \sigma_{2p_z}^1$$

  • Magnetic Nature: 1 unpaired electron $\rightarrow$ Paramagnetic.

  • HOMO Symmetry: The HOMO is the $\sigma_{2p_z}$ orbital. Since sigma orbitals are non-degenerate and possess cylindrical symmetry around the internuclear axis, a single electron here constitutes a symmetrical electronic distribution. (Condition Met)

  • $\mathrm{O}_2^{2-}$ ($18e^-$):

$$\dots \sigma_{2p_z}^2 (\pi_{2p_x}^2 = \pi_{2p_y}^2) (\pi_{2p_x}^{*2} = \pi_{2p_y}^{*2})$$

  • Magnetic Nature: 0 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ Diamagnetic. (Condition Not Met)

  • $\mathrm{C}_2$ ($12e^-$):

$$\dots \sigma_{2s}^2 \sigma_{2s}^{*2} (\pi_{2p_x}^2 = \pi_{2p_y}^2)$$

  • Magnetic Nature: 0 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ Diamagnetic. (Condition Not Met)

  • $\mathrm{O}_2$ ($16e^-$):

$$\dots \sigma_{2p_z}^2 (\pi_{2p_x}^2 = \pi_{2p_y}^2) (\pi_{2p_x}^{*1} = \pi_{2p_y}^{*1})$$

  • Magnetic Nature: 2 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ Paramagnetic.

  • HOMO Symmetry: The HOMO is the degenerate $\pi^*$ set. Each orbital holds exactly one electron, resulting in a symmetrically half-filled degenerate set. (Condition Met)

  • $\mathrm{B}_2$ ($10e^-$):

$$\dots \sigma_{2s}^2 \sigma_{2s}^{*2} (\pi_{2p_x}^1 = \pi_{2p_y}^1)$$

  • Magnetic Nature: 2 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ Paramagnetic.

  • HOMO Symmetry: The HOMO degenerate $\pi$ set is symmetrically half-filled with one electron in each orbital. (Condition Met)

  • $\mathrm{C}_2^{2-}$ ($14e^-$):

$$\dots \sigma_{2s}^2 \sigma_{2s}^{*2} (\pi_{2p_x}^2 = \pi_{2p_y}^2) \sigma_{2p_z}^2$$

  • Magnetic Nature: 0 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ Diamagnetic. (Condition Not Met)

  • $\mathrm{N}_2^{2-}$ ($16e^-$):

  • Isoelectronic with $\mathrm{O}_2$.

  • Magnetic Nature: 2 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ Paramagnetic.

  • HOMO Symmetry: Symmetrically half-filled $\pi^*$ degenerate orbitals. (Condition Met)

The species that are both paramagnetic and possess a symmetrical electronic distribution in their HOMO are $\mathrm{N}_2^+$, $\mathrm{O}_2$, $\mathrm{B}_2$, and $\mathrm{N}_2^{2-}$.

Total Number = 4

hi.content:
उन स्पीशीज की कुल संख्या जिनका/जिनके HOMO में सममित (symmetrical) इलेक्ट्रॉनिक वितरण है और साथ ही अनुचुंबकीय (paramagnetic) भी हैं।

$$ \mathrm{N}_2^{+}, \mathrm{O}_2^{2-}, \mathrm{C}_2, \mathrm{O}_2, \mathrm{~B}_2, \mathrm{C}_2^{2-}, \mathrm{N}_2^{2-} $$
